articles.title: Tove Jansson's Works and Loves
articles.description: What's in an artist? From what do they fashion their work? In their new retrospective exhibition on Finnish author and illustrator Tove Jansson (1914-2001), the Quentin Blake Center for Illustration sets out to answer these perennial questions by looking not only at the artist but the people who surrounded her. The newly announced exhibit, titled "Tove Jansson and her Families," will feature previously unseen drawings and is "the UK's first ever exhibition to focus on Tove Jansson's work as an illustrator," and runs from Nov. 21, 2026, to May 9, 2027. Most famous for her work on the Moomins, hippopotamus-like creatures both endearing and blunt, Jansson illustrated extensively for numerous magazines and wrote novels such as The Summer Book and Fair Play outside her books for children. In the spirit of this retrospective exhibition, I too wanted to reflect on Jansson's work in the quarter-century after her passing in 2001. Jansson's childhood Tove Jansson was born to sculptor Viktor Jansson and graphic designer Signe Hammersten-Jansson in a Swedish-speaking minority within Helsinki, Finland. With a father whose sculptural work is still on display in her hometown, and a mother who "designed most of Finland's postage stamps from 1929 until 1962," Jansson was exposed to aesthetic, bohemian influences from an incredibly early age. The Quentin Blake Center's exhibition will include some of Jansson's earliest humorous magazines and booklets which she sold to her classmates starting from the age of seven. Her tendency towards satire began early too. According to Jansson's biographer Tuula Karjalainen, she was reprimanded at 12 years old "for drawing a caricature of her teacher on the class black-board." At 16, Jansson went on to study art in Stockholm. While her parents' artistic influences followed her her entire life, she was also exposed to a great drive towards Modernism in the art world of the Finnish 1930s. The Moomins In addition to exhibiting her early satirical and comic works, the Quentin Blake Center's exhibition features art depicting " the origins of the beloved Moomins. " The Moomins' origins appeared in political cartoons which Jansson drew for Finnish anti-fascist left-wing magazine Garm during her teenage years. According to Kathryn Davis' introduction to Jansson's The Summer Book , an even earlier version appeared as an "insulting portrait of Immanuel Kant... on an outhouse wall after she lost a philosophical quarrel with one of her brothers." Jansson would continue to illustrate for Garm until the end of its publication in 1953, contributing " around five hundred drawings... including every single cover from 1944 onwards ." In her illustrations for Garm , a Moomin-like, long-snouted creature would accompany her signatures. They thus represented Jansson herself, but they would also appear in her more grim, private work to represent "ghostlike and scary creatures... released from the shadowy forces of the subconscious." Yet during World War II, she began to reimagine the Moomins in a world of their own, and "through them she escaped " into the idyllic valley of her children's stories. But the Moomins were not characters typically featured in magically happy children's books. It was important for Jansson to include more strife and more reality, wishing not "to shut out the mystery, tenderness and cruelty that were a part of the child's world." She may have wanted to escape from the war, but she did not want to deceive herself, nor anyone else. Children, like the main character Moomin or the mischievous Little My, are clever and rambunctious. Indeed, the characters of Moominvalley "often [say] rude things and even [swear] at times." They may not be role models, but they are funny and endearing. Biographical Influences Moreover, the Moomins and Jansson's other work often reflected the people in her own life. Family is central to the Moomins in particular. The main family consisting of Moomin, also known as Moomintroll, Moominmama and Moominpapa took after Jansson's own family. Jansson saw herself in the precocious Little My as well as in Moomin himself. Moomin's best friend, the gruff, always-traveling Snufkin, takes after Finnish left-wing intellectual Atos Wirtanen, whom Jansson was in love with and briefly engaged to. Leaving Moomin and Moominvalley every winter to travel south, Snufkin parallels Wirtanen's absenteeism and need to be alone. Thus left behind, Moomin gave voice to his author's love and love troubles : "Moomintroll, who waited and yearned so terribly. Who sat there at home, waiting and admiring, and who said: Of course you should be free. It's obvious that you need to go away. And I understand that you have to be alone sometimes. And at the same time Moomintroll's eyes were dark with disappointment and helpless longing." Jansson's other works, such as The Summer Book and Fair Play , are equally influenced by her family and loved ones. The Summer Book , written one year after the death of Jansson's mother Signe Hammersten-Jansson, is immanent with quiet grief. The story, a series of vignettes, is set on an island on which a grandmother and her six-year-old granddaughter Sophia live after the death of the latter's mother. They go about exploring the island, observing the animals, writing stories and talking to each other. The two discuss death with a funny casualness which only the very young and very old can manage. A daughter figuring out how to live without a mother, Jansson imbues The Summer Book with the striving working through of loss. Similarly set on an island, Fair Play captures the serene love between two elderly women, the artist Jonna and the writer Mari. The story is inspired by Jansson's own relationship to her life partner and lover Tuulikki Pietilä, one of Finland's most influential graphic artists who taught at the Academy of Fine Arts, Helsinki. Like Jansson and Pietilä - who "spent every summer for nearly 30 years" on a " tiny barren island no bigger than a football pitch" - Jonna and Mari work on their crafts and their relationship with each other. Work and Love Tuula Karjalainen's biography on Jansson is titled Tove Jansson: Work and Love , named after Jansson's motto: Laborare et Amare. Through her career, Jansson shows that love and work are more than two separate practices to alternate between, but rather two things mutually influencing one another. Her work is full of the people whom she loved, and who loved her in return. Published at a tumultuously political time, the Moomins drew criticism for "portraying an excessively bourgeois view of the family." It's true that Moominpapa, Moominmama, and Moomin live lives befitting traditional familial and gender roles. Yet their inclusion of and community with other characters, as well as Jansson's own nontraditional life, points toward the flourishing of multiple families, families beyond the family, as circles around one, enriching one's own work and love.

articles.title: Kodiak Sciences presenteert maandag resultaten fase 3-studie
There's a New Way to Break RSA Encryption
articles.description: "Signature forgery." It's a new way to break RSA keys — and it doesn't require factoring. Ars Technica reports on new research using classical computing to "reduce the current RSA security level to an unacceptably low threshold" and lower the required computing resources by orders of magnitude. There's "a gap in current RSA-type security assumptions," according to a paper co-authored by University of California, San Diego professor Nadia Heninger, who argues that gap "gives classical cryptanalytic evidence in favor of moving away from RSA entirely during the current post-quantum transition." The practical risk is limited, but still significant. Applying the attack against the deprecated use of 1024-bit keys took a handful of months on an academic CPU cluster, significantly less than the current estimates for 1024-bit factoring that would require resources that only nations or companies with massive resources could achieve. Widely used RSA implementations are also safe. Nonetheless, the research has taken cryptographers by surprise... "If this result holds up under peer review, it would indeed be a conceptual break-through," Karsten Nohl, a cryptography expert and the head of innovation at Allurity, said in an interview. "RSA is as difficult to break as it is to factor large integers, at least so we thought. The researcher suggests that you can practically break RSA without cracking its key...." The key forgery attack Heninger and the other researchers devised poses an immediate threat to 1024-bit RSA. Even for 2048- and 4096-bit keys, the method reduces the security of RSA to unacceptable levels. The National Security Agency, National Institute of Standards and Technology, and European Union Agency for Network and Information Security require that any cryptosystem should provide a level of no less than 128 or more bits, meaning the operations required must exceed 2**128. The forgery attack drops these levels to 2**65, 2**90, and 2**119 for 1024-, 2048-, and 4096-bit keys respectively. These levels may further drop because Heninger's team did all the coding by hand and used no AI or GPUs in performing the forgeries. The researcher said these tools will "almost certainly" drop the security levels further. The attack works only against blind-signature implementations of RSA... Still, some real-world systems continue to use blind-signature, also known as textbook, RSA... The paper's authors and other researchers stress that the new attack poses little real-world threat. It does, however, drastically lower the estimated security of textbook RSA, and it does so in a way no one knew of previously... The new attack will further increase the urgency of completely moving away from the cryptosystem. Thanks to long-time Slashdot reader phatrabt for sharing the article. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Yeast could be the key to building the first Martian cities
articles.description: Building a human civilization on Mars will be orders of magnitude harder than any of the human migrations on Earth ever were. Here, you can build refuge anywhere, which is why our civilization is everywhere from pole to pole. If we ever hope to live on the red planet, we must build with the red dirt right beneath our boots, a challenge that has long been thought to demand expensive, huge industrial machinery and nuclear plant-level power generation. Now, a team of researchers has unveiled a radical, low-energy alternative in which a crew could carry a tiny tube of dormant yeast from Earth, breed trillions of helper cells in a vat using Martian carbon dioxide and melted ground ice, and 3D print entire outposts using modest solar power. The new approach, led by Jishen Qiu at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and detailed in a study published in Chem Circularity , uses the freezing Martian climate to its advantage. Instead of melting rock, the team created what they call a “Martian living building material” by blending sand with a water-based binder made of pig-derived gelatin and genetically modified yeast. When extruded and exposed to simulated Martian surface conditions—temperatures averaging minus 85 degrees Fahrenheit and an atmosphere roughly a hundred times thinner than Earth’s—the material freezes and dehydrates on its own. The physical results are competitive with conventional construction products. The composite achieves an average compressive strength of about 12 megapascals, placing it alongside standard lightweight concrete, while its flexural strength—how well a material resists snapping under bending pressure—reaches 6 megapascals. That high flexural strength means the material resists bending and tension twice as well as typical lightweight concrete, a critical trait for surviving high-velocity debris hurled by Martian sandstorms. At the same time, producing 1 cubic meter (35 cubic feet) of the biocomposite demands tens of times less material processing energy than sintering, or baking mineral grains together with intense heat, running on less than an hour of standard solar power rather than days of continuous heating. This solution is not without challenges and roadblocks, but it beats the alternatives so far. The leading blueprints for Martian construction have relied on brute force. Most proposals center on sintering, a technique that blasts loose Martian regolith—the powdery soil and broken rock covering the planet’s surface—with lasers, microwaves, or giant solar kilns to melt it into ceramic blocks. The drawback is severe: Melting rock requires temperatures exceeding 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit. Powering that kind of heat demands nuclear reactors or massive solar arrays running for weeks just to produce enough material for a basic outpost. The resulting ceramic is brittle, cracks easily under bending loads, and cannot be recycled once damaged. It’s extremely hard to do. Other options include going underground or into mountains like Tolkien dwarves. These are also extremely expensive, requiring huge machinery and energy bills. That could be the way to go for the far future but—at least for the first waves of colonists—we need a lighter and more affordable solution. Genetic Engineering Is the Key The secret behind the material’s strength lies in genetic modification—turning ordinary baker’s yeast into living, microscopic construction workers. Natural yeast cells are simple, smooth spheres, but Qiu’s team modified their DNA to sprout three distinct tools on their outer skins. First, they added AGA2, a surface protein that acts like an anchor to tether the cells directly to sand grains. Second, they engineered the cells to produce mussel foot proteins—synthetic replicas of the supersticky glue sea mussels use to grip wave-battered rocks underwater. Third, they added a paired protein system called SpyTag and SpyCatcher; like microscopic Velcro, the two parts snap together the instant they touch, forming permanent chemical bonds that lock neighboring yeast cells together into an unbroken web. When that paste exits a 3D printer nozzle heated to a warm 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit—normal human body temperature—it hits the bitter cold of Mars. Normally, freezing water expands into large, dagger-like ice crystals that would tear the material apart. Instead, the protein coats on the yeast act as microscopic traffic cops, forcing the ice to freeze into an orderly grid of tiny, 5-micrometer pockets. Because the Martian atmosphere is a razor-thin quasi vacuum, that ice never melts; it sublimates, evaporating directly from solid ice into gas. Once the moisture vanishes into thin air, it leaves behind a lightweight, sponge-like skeleton of animal gelatin, with the embedded yeast acting like steel rods inside concrete slabs to keep the walls from collapsing. As a bonus, this is all recyclable. The researchers tested the cured bricks to the breaking point by crushing them under heavy hydraulic presses. But then they didn’t throw out the rubble. They gently warmed the debris back into a spreadable paste and 3D printed brand-new structural blocks through four consecutive generations. The recycled bricks suffered zero loss in compressive strength or stiffness, and the internal yeast cells emerged alive and kicking every single time. Solvable Roadblocks Despite the laboratory success, taking this technology out of the environmental chamber and onto the Martian surface presents hurdles that Qiu acknowledges need to be solved. The most immediate technical limitation is that the highest-performing formula still relies on porcine gelatin imported from Earth, he tells me in an email interview. To achieve true independence, the yeast must synthesize the entire structural scaffold on its own, cutting out animal products entirely. When I asked Qiu why the yeast cannot yet replace pig gelatin, he explained that the issue isn’t whether the biological glue holds up. The glue sticks, but the cells do not yet churn out enough physical volume of protein to form the shock-absorbing lattice needed to distribute structural loads evenly across the sand. Water management poses another operational dilemma. Because the bricks harden through open-air freeze-drying, moisture sublimates directly into the thin Martian atmosphere—a daunting trade-off in a world where every liter of water is vital for drinking and rocket propellant. To prevent that loss, Qiu suggests that the entire printing and curing process could move inside a lightweight air dome so the evaporated water can be trapped and recycled—though he doesn’t view water consumption as a dealbreaker, since vast reserves of surface ice are available in several regions of Mars. Then there are the thorny issues of biology and planetary law. Because the engineered yeast survives the freeze-drying process fully viable, unleashing it on Mars directly bumps up against the planetary protection mandates of NASA and the international Committee on Space Research that are designed to keep alien environments free of terrestrial biological contamination. The reality is that, once we put boots up there, the mandates are going out the hatch. The day living astronauts step out of a lander, trillions of skin and gut microbes arrive with them, making construction yeast just one piece of a much larger containment puzzle . As Qiu points out, “as long as human beings landed, there would be a good chance that the microbes in our body may be exposed to the atmosphere there.” The final roadblock to using organic material to create Martian habitats is the brutal bath of unshielded cosmic radiation sweeping the red landscape. Prolonged radiation could mutate or destroy organisms, and Qiu acknowledges that they haven’t tested yet for the resistance of the yeast. Yet he is confident that synthetic biology already has an answer waiting in nature. “We are sure that some microbes can do it and can also be genetically engineered for similar purposes, like making mechanical proteins,” he says. A lot has to happen between these experiments and actual colonization—like the spaceships to take us there, everything is still a sci-fi fantasy —but the research ultimately demonstrates that off-world construction does not have to rely on heavy industrial kilns. By substituting massive thermal energy with programmable cellular biology, future explorers might construct permanent shelters from little more than dirt, ice, and a tube of living organisms.

articles.title: Events this weekend (Sept. 26-27)
articles.description: Events this weekend (Sept. 26-27) From comic books and outdoor movies to handmade crafts, astrology and neighborhood celebrations, this weekend offers a mix of creative and community events across Baltimore. Saturday brings the Baltimore Comic-Con, a screening of Dirty Dancing under the stars and a local makers market, while Sunday features hands-on sewing, an astrology workshop and the Abell Community Street Fair. Saturday, September 26 Baltimore Comic-Con, Baltimore Convention Center, Sept. 25-27 The Baltimore Comic-Con returns to the Baltimore Convention Center for a weekend celebrating comic books, creators and pop culture. Attendees can meet artists and publishers, browse vendors, and participate in drop-in art workshops. The convention runs Friday through Sunday, with Sunday programming beginning at 10 a.m. Silent Movie Night: Dirty Dancing , Canton Waterfront Park, 7-10 p.m. Watch Dirty Dancing under the stars at Canton Waterfront Park during a special Rhythm & Reels Silent Movie Night . Attendees can follow the movie through event-provided headphones while enjoying the waterfront atmosphere. The event will also feature free popcorn with a gourmet toppings bar and a loaded baked potato bar from Raspberry Moments. Admission is $10 per person. Mini Maker's Market - It's Fall, Y'all!, R. House, 12-6 p.m. Head to R. House for the Mini Maker's Market - It's Fall, Y'all , a fall-themed afternoon featuring handmade goods, local crafts and food vendors. Shoppers can browse everything from candles and jewelry to ceramics, artwork and crochet pieces while supporting Baltimore-area makers. Admission is free. Sunday, September 27 Live Patch Sewing Event by The Flying Puffin, The Charmers Club, 11 a.m.-4 p.m. Stop by The Charmers Club for a hands-on customization event with The Flying Puffin. Choose a tote bag or clothing piece or bring in an item of your own, and personalize it with your choice of patches. Pricing varies depending on the item and customization. The Astrological Sun: Getting to Know Your Sun Sign, Manor Mill, 1-3 p.m. Explore the meaning of the Sun in astrology during this interactive class with ODastrology . The session will examine how the Sun relates to autonomy, creativity, self-expression and life purpose, including how it can manifest across different signs. Tickets are $40, and attendees should bring a pen and paper and provide their birth information when registering. Abell Community Street Fair: "Over the Moon," Abell Avenue & 32nd Street, 12-5 p.m. Celebrate the Abell community at its annual street fair, this year inspired by sci-fi and outer space. The event will feature a silent auction, porch concerts, local food and drinks, art, costumes, and neighborhood decorations. Admission is free, and proceeds support the Abell Improvement Association's year-round community projects.
